opus-5.5.text:
Well, I should start by saying I have enormous respect for Eliezer. He was thinking seriously about AI alignment twenty years before almost anyone else, back when it was considered a fringe obsession, and a lot of what's now mainstream in the field traces back to him. So I don't dismiss his concerns at all.

But where I part ways is on the level of certainty. Eliezer's position, as I understand it, is that if we build something smarter than us with anything like current techniques, then by default everyone dies, with very high probability. My problem is that I just don't think we know enough to be that confident about *anything* here, in either direction. We're in a situation of deep uncertainty. Nobody predicted that you'd get something like GPT by just scaling up next-token prediction. If our track record on forecasting this stuff is that poor, then I think the right epistemic stance is humility, not "we're doomed with 99% probability."

And then there's the practical side. Suppose you did want an internationally enforced moratorium. Eliezer has been admirably honest that this would potentially mean being willing to use force against data centers in countries that don't comply. When you think through what that actually entails, the geopolitical risks, the risk of it driving development underground or into the hands of the least careful actors, it's not obvious to me that it reduces existential risk rather than adding new kinds of it.

There's also an opportunity cost that I think gets underweighted. AI could help with drug discovery, with science, with all sorts of problems that are themselves matters of life and death. A blanket shutdown forgoes all of that, based on an argument whose premises I find genuinely uncertain.

What I'd rather see, and part of why I took the leave to work on this at OpenAI, is people actually trying to make progress on alignment as a science, with concrete problems you can get feedback on: interpretability, watermarking, understanding how these models generalize. In my experience, the way you make progress on hard problems is by engaging with the actual systems, not by deciding in advance that the problem is hopeless. If at some point we get real evidence that we're heading off a cliff, if we see systems deceiving us in dangerous ways or capabilities we can't evaluate, then I'm open to much stronger measures. I'm not an accelerationist. I just think the case for slamming on the brakes worldwide, right now, hasn't been made with the kind of evidence that would justify the costs.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, let me start by saying that I take Eliezer much more seriously than most of my academic colleagues do. I spent two years at OpenAI thinking about alignment, and I came away convinced that the people worried about this are not crazy. I don't think the probability of catastrophe is zero. If you told me it was five or ten percent over this century, I wouldn't laugh.

But that's exactly the crux. Eliezer's position is something like ninety-nine percent. He treats doom as close to a theorem, as if we've already proven that any sufficiently capable system optimizing for anything will kill us all. And I just don't see the proof. I see a lot of plausible arguments, a lot of thought experiments about orthogonality and instrumental convergence, but when I look at what has actually happened with large language models, it doesn't look like the scenario he spent fifteen years warning about. These systems absorbed human values as a byproduct of absorbing human text. They're weird and they're fallible, but they are not alien paperclip maximizers. Reality has not yet confirmed the picture, and I think a rationalist ought to update on that.

So then the question is: what do you do when you're in a state of real uncertainty? And here's where the policy proposal falls apart for me. "Shut it all down, enforced internationally, be willing to bomb the data centers," that's not a policy, it's a wish. There is no mechanism in the world today that could make that happen. You'd need the US, China, and every other major player to agree, to verify each other, and to give up what they each perceive as a decisive strategic advantage. We couldn't even do that for nuclear weapons, where the thing you're worried about is a physical device that leaves a radioactive signature. Here the thing you're worried about is matrix multiplication.

And I worry about the counterfactual. If the responsible actors stop, the technology doesn't stop. It just gets built by the people who weren't going to listen anyway, and the folks who actually cared about safety have removed themselves from the room. I'd rather have the alignment researchers inside these companies, with access to the frontier models, than have them standing outside holding signs.

The other thing, and I'll say this gently because I respect him, is that Eliezer's framework is unfalsifiable in a way that makes me nervous. Every encouraging observation gets reinterpreted as the AI being deceptive, or as evidence that we just haven't hit the dangerous capability threshold yet. There's no experiment you could run that would make him say "okay, I was wrong." And when a worldview has that property, I think you should be more careful, not less, about letting it dictate drastic action.

So my position is kind of boring by comparison. I think we should do the interpretability research, the evals, the watermarking, the dangerous capability testing. I think it's fine to have regulation, maybe even licensing for the biggest training runs. I'd love it if the labs moved slower. But "pause everything globally or we all die" is a conclusion that outruns the evidence, and the enforcement mechanism it requires doesn't exist. I'm not going to pretend otherwise just because the stakes are high. If anything, high stakes are a reason to think more carefully, not to grab the most dramatic answer on the table.

astra-6.text:
Well, I take seriously the possibility that advanced AI could pose an existential risk. But there’s a substantial gap between taking that possibility seriously and concluding that an internationally enforced shutdown of further scaling is the right response.

There are really two questions here. One is how confident we should be that continued development leads to catastrophe. The other is whether a shutdown would actually produce a safer world. Even if you’re very worried about the first, you still have to answer the second: How would the agreement be verified? How would it handle violations? Who would decide which research could continue, and on what evidence would we ever restart?

My uncertainty cuts both ways. We don’t have a convincing argument that sufficiently powerful AI will be safe. But I also don’t think we have a convincing argument that alignment is hopeless, or that further empirical work can’t substantially improve our position. I’m wary of treating either conclusion as something we’ve already established.

And there are potential benefits that matter enormously—scientific discoveries, treatments for diseases, tools that help us understand and solve other problems. Those don’t automatically outweigh an existential risk. But they do belong in the calculation.

So I’m much more sympathetic to demanding safety evaluations, investing heavily in alignment, and imposing restrictions when there’s concrete evidence of dangerous capabilities. I could support a pause under sufficiently alarming circumstances. Where I part company is with the certainty that we already know enough to make a globally enforced shutdown our overriding objective.

sol-6.1.text:
I take the possibility of catastrophic AI risk seriously. Where I part company with Eliezer is in the confidence of the argument: that continued scaling will lead to systems that kill everyone, and that an internationally enforced shutdown is therefore our best option. There are enormous uncertainties in both halves of that claim.

We don’t have a theory that lets us reliably predict what the next few generations of AI will be capable of, much less what goals they’ll pursue or how successfully we’ll be able to control them. That uncertainty is a reason to do safety research and to be willing to impose restrictions. But I don’t think it automatically singles out a worldwide shutdown as the right policy.

You also have to ask how such an agreement would work. How would you verify compliance? What happens if some countries comply and others don’t? What powers would you need to enforce it, and what risks would those powers create? Those are part of the safety calculation too.

My inclination is to pursue technical safety work, evaluations, and governance that can respond to evidence—and to preserve the option of stopping if the evidence warrants it. I’m not confident that everything will be fine. I’m also not confident enough in a particular catastrophe scenario to endorse the remedy Eliezer advocates.
